searchText: Listening to the ASE call, I have a question: How important is it that we allow legacy contracts to be able to interact with long addresses? It seems that a really simple approach without all the complexities would be to just disallow legacy contracts from touching accounts with long addresses. The drawback is of course that it would be more and more expensive to interact with legacy contracts when we start expiring state, until the legacy contract upgrades. There needs to be some way otherwise it is like launching a brand new network. The ideas we thought about so far: translation map, migration (contracts to upgrade their bytecode), or some bridge-like mechanism. <@425279588009246720> With Firefox, each browser *window* shows up as a different target for sharing in Zoom. I'm guessing you were using another browser, that perhaps registers each window differently with the OS? Or perhaps it was an OS difference, I'm on Windows, but maybe Mac or Linux have different window management primitives. Had Safari open as yet to install a proper browser 😬 1. Install OS. 2. Install a new browser. 3. Install everything else. Perhaps you were between 1 and 2 at the time the call started though? Unfortunate timing if so. Is there a recording of this mornings call? cc: <@!642887713246150666> i believe The video is currently processing. It will be added to Stateless Ethereum meetings playlist (https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL4cwHXAawZxpUwQhkP_Np8eDY6jFCfxs6) Contract interactions aren't linear enough in modern defi for that to work. For example, Uniswap v3 swaps work by sending you the tokens you bought, calling a callback you provided and then reverting the entire transaction if the tokens haven't been paid for when the callback returns. Working Group: Address Space Extension Meeting https://youtu.be/HSEEjoljb6g
